KEY MESSAGE 1...A strong coastal storm is expected to bring 
significant impacts to the region starting late Wednesday night, 
peaking during Thanksgiving Day, and departing into Friday.

Following a period of relatively benign weather, our attention 
turns to the coastal storm arriving for the holiday. Beginning 
on Wednesday, the storm of concern will begin to take shape off 
the Southeast coast.

Synoptics:

A strong upper-low will shift eastward out of the central US, with 
strong divergence aloft favoring surface cyclogenesis just off the 
southeast coast. From there, the low is expected to track northward 
towards the Mid Atlantic through Thursday. Guidance remains quite 
consistent on the development and rapid deepening of this low, and 
has come into better agreement as far as timing and the storm track. 
The GFS, RGEM, and ECMWF all track the low northward from the coast 
of the Carolinas northward towards western PA. 

A ~1044 mb high will be in place near the Gulf of Maine Wednesday 
night, which will shift eastward toward Nova Scotia into Thursday. 
Meanwhile, the ~1000 mb surface low will race northward into 
Thursday. This will create a very strong pressure gradient across 
our region, with surface pressure falls of near 35 mb in 24 hours 
(greater than 1 mb/hour). A powerful low level jet is forecast to 
develop in response ahead of the low and sweep northward along the 
coast, with 925 mb winds in the 70-80 kts range. Notably, the 925 mb 
level is below the marine layer inversion, however the mixed 
boundary layer will be shallower than this (~1000 feet deep or so). 
Even then, GFS BUFKIT profiles indicate winds speeds within the 
mixed layer in the 50-60 kts range across the coastal plain of NJ 
and Delmarva, and in the 45-55 knot range as far inland as the 
Philly metro and portions of northern NJ. Further inland from there, 
boundary layer wind speeds look to peak around 35-45 kts. 

Impacts:

Specific impacts continue to come into better focus.

Precip type: The chance for wintry precipitation (even at onset) is 
low, even across the Poconos and adjacent portions of far northern 
NJ. Precipitation onset now could be as late as Thursday afternoon 
for these locations, and warm air advection will have been underway 
for quite some time by that point with surface temperatures well 
above freezing. This currently appears to be an all rain event for 
all locations within our coverage area.

Winds: Our biggest concerns with this storm are high winds and 
coastal flooding (see coastal flooding key message below). Northeast 
to east winds will begin ramping up Wednesday night before peaking 
Thursday. Gusts of 50 to 60 mph are likely inland across our entire 
area, with gusts potentially reaching near 70 mph along the Atlantic 
coast and Delaware Bay coast. Sustained winds along the immediate 
coast could exceed 40 mph. The High Wind Watch was upgraded to a 
High Wind Warning for our coastal counties northward through Kent 
County MD and DE as these are the areas we have the greatest 
confidence in winds gusting up to 60 mph. North of here the High 
Wind Watch remains in effect for southeast PA northward into 
portions of central NJ. The Watches and Warnings are valid starting 
late evening evening into the overnight Wednesday night through 
Thursday evening. Widespread tree damage and power outages will be 
possible across much of our area, especially toward the coast. The 
winds are expected to subside overnight Thursday night, however some 
guidance suggests southwest to west winds will increase with gusts 
near 40 to 50 mph possible again Friday afternoon and evening.

Rain: Given recent dryness and the progressive nature of this 
system, freshwater flooding does not appear to be as significant of 
a concern, but this threat will continue to be monitored as rainfall 
amounts come into better focus. A general 1.25 - 2.5 inches of rain 
is forecast, though some localized amounts up to 3" could occur near 
the coast. The Weather Prediction Center has the area in a MARGINAL 
risk for excessive rainfall. Any flooding impacts should be confined 
mainly to urban flooding and flooding of low lying, poor drainage 
areas, as well as some of our more sensitive streams and creeks. The 
heavy rainfall could also exacerbate coastal flooding issues. Some 
light rain may linger on Friday, especially northwest of I-95, but 
any rainfall on Friday will be inconsequential.

Timing: The greatest storm impacts from high winds and rain look to 
be during the daytime period Thursday into Thursday evening, with 
the low pulling away from the area on Friday. As far as onset 
timing, models have come into better overall agreement in rain 
beginning overnight Wednesday night over portions of Delmarva into 
southern NJ, around dawn near Philly, and potentially not until the 
early afternoon over the Poconos into NW NJ. The winds will begin 
ramping up though before the rain arrives with winds likely peaking
